function renderQuestWidget() { const containers = document.querySelectorAll('.daily-quests-container, #daily-quests-root'); if (containers.length === 0) return; const quests = getDailyQuests(); containers.forEach(container => { container.innerHTML = \`

Today's Daily Quests

\${new Date().toLocaleDateString('en-US', { weekday: 'short', month: 'short', day: 'numeric' })}
\${quests.map(q => \`
\${q.title} +\${q.xp} XP

\${q.desc}

\${q.completed ? '' : '' + q.current + '/' + q.target + ''}
\`).join('')}
\`; }); }

const grammarTerms = [
    {

        name: "Appositives & Renaming Phrases",

        grade: 5,
        gradeName: "5th Grade",
        branch: "clauses-phrases",

        formula: "Noun + , [Appositive Phrase] , + Predicate",
        rawFormula: "Noun + , [Appositive Phrase] , + Rest of Sentence",
        definition: "A noun or noun phrase placed immediately adjacent to another noun to rename, amplify, or clarify its identity, typically enclosed within commas if non-essential.",
        whatItDoes: "It adds concise descriptive clarity without forcing the writer to construct a separate, clunky relative clause.",
        howToDoIt: [
            "Identify the anchor noun that requires identification or description.",
            "Formulate a renaming noun phrase directly following the anchor noun.",
            "Determine essentiality: if the phrase is non-restrictive (extra info), enclose it in commas; if restrictive (vital to identify who/what), omit commas."
        ],
        exampleProblem: "Combine into one concise sentence using an appositive: 'Dr. Katherine Johnson was a pioneering NASA mathematician. She calculated orbital flight paths.'",
        exampleSolution: "'Dr. Katherine Johnson, a pioneering NASA mathematician, calculated orbital flight paths.' (The appositive 'a pioneering NASA mathematician' renames Dr. Johnson).",
        codexChapter: 5,
        keywords: "appositive noun phrase commas punctuation non-essential restrictive grade 5"

    {
        id: "g11-balanced-periodic",

        branch: "sentence-structures",
        branchLabel: "Sentence Structures",
        formula: "[Subordinate Elements / Dependent Clauses] ... + Main Independent Clause .",
        rawFormula: "[Modifiers / Clauses] ... -> Main Clause at the Period",
        definition: "A deliberate syntactic construction where the main grammatical clause and core rhetorical meaning are suspended until the terminal end (the period), preceded by introductory modifiers.",
        whatItDoes: "It builds rhetorical anticipation, syntactic tension, and climatic emphasis, compelling the reader to absorb supporting conditions before the resolving revelation.",
        howToDoIt: [
            "Draft the primary independent clause representing your focal revelation.",
            "Prepend subordinate clauses, participial phrases, or prepositional chains.",
            "Withhold the governing subject and finite verb until right before the closing punctuation mark."
        ],
        exampleProblem: "Transform the loose sentence 'He finally discovered the cure after years of tireless research in cold laboratories.' into a periodic sentence.",
        exampleSolution: "'After years of tireless research and countless bitter setbacks in cold, solitary laboratories, he finally discovered the cure.' (Suspends the resolution until the terminal predicate).",
        codexChapter: 11,
        keywords: "periodic sentence balanced sentence rhetorical syntax climax suspense grade 11"
    },
    {
        id: "g7-comma-splices",
        name: "Comma Splices & Run-On Remediation",
        etymology: "/ˈkɒm.ə splaɪs/ • Middle English: \"splisen\" (to join ends together)",
        grade: 7,
        gradeName: "7th Grade",
        branch: "syntactic-pitfalls",
        branchLabel: "Syntactic Pitfalls",
        formula: "Independent Clause + , [Coordinating Conjunction (FANBOYS)] + Independent Clause",
        rawFormula: "IC + , + FANBOYS + IC  OR  IC + ; + IC",
        definition: "A widespread mechanical error where two independent clauses are joined solely with a comma without an accompanying coordinating conjunction or appropriate punctuation mark.",
        whatItDoes: "It confuses sentence boundaries by tricking the reader into expecting a continuation rather than a complete, self-sustaining grammatical statement.",
        howToDoIt: [
            "Test both sides of the comma: if each side contains a subject and finite verb and can stand alone as a sentence, you have a comma splice.",
            "Fix 1: Insert a coordinating conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) after the comma.",
            "Fix 2: Replace the comma with a semicolon (;).",

        exampleProblem: "Identify and rectify the error: 'The storm knocked down power lines, the whole neighborhood was dark.'",
        exampleSolution: "Error: Comma splice. Rectification: 'The storm knocked down power lines, and the whole neighborhood was dark.' OR 'The storm knocked down power lines; the whole neighborhood was dark.'",
